relations.note: Imhotep is repeatedly called the son of Ptah.
Late monuments name the human or divinized Khereduankh as Imhotep's mother.
Some theological schemes make Ptah's consort Sekhmet the mother of Imhotep.
One unstable late tradition presents Renpetneferet as Imhotep's sister.
An alternative unstable tradition presents Renpetneferet as Imhotep's wife.
The deceased sage is invoked in a transfigured Osirian form as Sokar-Osiris Imhotep.

relations.myth: Imhotep discovers Khnum's authority over the Nile
relations.note: Imhotep consults sacred records and identifies Khnum as controller of the Nile.

relations.myth: Elephantine gods appear in the famine narrative
relations.note: Satis shares the Elephantine theology and offering scene without directly interacting with Imhotep.

relations.myth: Elephantine gods appear in the famine narrative
relations.note: Anuket shares the Elephantine theology and offering scene without directly interacting with Imhotep.

relations.myth: Imhotep enters Thoth's theology of sacred writing
relations.note: Priestly texts associate Imhotep with Thoth's scribal knowledge and divine books.
Greek cult and literary sources explicitly identify Imouthes with the healing god Asklepios.
Greek interpretive texts call Imouthes-Asklepios son of Hephaistos, translating his filiation to Ptah.

relations.myth: Joint worship of two deified sages
relations.note: Imhotep and Amenhotep son of Hapu received paired worship at Deir el-Bahari.

relations.myth: Imhotep worshipped within Isis's Philae sanctuary
relations.note: Imhotep received offerings in a chapel under Isis's overarching temple authority.

relations.myth: Possible impersonation in the Edfu sacred drama
relations.note: A lector-priest may have impersonated Imhotep in Horus's drama, though the reconstruction is debated.
